concepts_used: Article 358 vs Article 359: Automatic Suspension vs Presidential Order

solution.concept_anchor: Article 359 suspends enforcement not the right itself
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students commonly recall that Article 359 'suspends Fundamental Rights' without distinguishing between the right and the right to approach courts for its enforcement.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Article 359 does not suspend the Fundamental Right itself — it suspends the right to move courts for its enforcement; the FR technically continues to exist.
Eliminate (b): Article 358 operates automatically upon proclamation; it requires no Presidential Order — only Article 359 requires a Presidential Order.
Eliminate (d): Article 359 can apply to most FRs under Part III but Articles 20 and 21 are explicitly excluded — the option is therefore incorrect.

Confirm (c): Article 359 requires a Presidential Order specifying which FRs are affected, and it is the right of enforcement (not the FR) that is suspended — this is the precise constitutional position.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The most common confusion here is treating 'suspension of the right to move courts' as equivalent to 'suspension of the Fundamental Right.' Under Article 359, the FR itself is not erased — it merely becomes unenforceable in courts for the duration of the Presidential Order. A student who has memorised that 'Article 359 suspends FRs' will choose option (a) confidently, missing the crucial philosophical and constitutional distinction that the 44th Amendment underscores.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 358 and 359 are the two constitutional provisions governing FR suspension during National Emergency, but they operate very differently. Article 358 is automatic — upon proclamation of emergency due to war or external aggression, Article 19 freedoms stand suspended without any further order. Article 359, by contrast, requires the President to issue a specific order naming the FRs that cannot be enforced.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Article 359 suspends the right to move courts for enforcement, not the Fundamental Right itself. The FR continues to exist in theory.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Article 358 is self-executing and requires no Presidential Order. Only Article 359 requires such an order.
• Option (c) — Correct: This precisely captures the Article 359 mechanism — a Presidential Order suspends the right to seek judicial enforcement of specified FRs.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Articles 20 and 21 are constitutionally immune from suspension under Article 359 after the 44th Amendment 1978.

Value Addition:
• Article 358 affects only Article 19; Article 359 can affect any FR except Articles 20 and 21.
• Article 359 suspension can be limited to part of India's territory.
• The 44th Amendment 1978 was the legislative response to the ADM Jabalpur judgment of 1976.

solution.concept_anchor: 44th Amendment makes Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable

statement_analysis.statement: Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even by a Presidential Order under Article 359 during National Emergency.
statement_analysis.reason: The 44th Amendment Act 1978 explicitly made Articles 20 and 21 immune from suspension under Article 359, directly correcting the constitutional gap exposed by the ADM Jabalpur judgment.

statement_analysis.statement: The 44th Amendment Act 1978 was enacted in direct response to the Supreme Court's ruling in ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla, which had permitted suspension of Article 21.
statement_analysis.reason: ADM Jabalpur (1976) allowed detention without any enforceable right to life during emergency; the 44th Amendment constitutionally overrode this by making Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable.

statement_analysis.statement: Even Parliament, through a constitutional amendment, can authorise the suspension of Articles 20 and 21 during a National Emergency.
statement_analysis.reason: Making Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable is considered part of the basic structure; moreover, Article 359 explicitly carves them out — Parliament cannot legislate around this exclusion even during emergency.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All three' feels correct because statements 1 and 2 are both accurate, and students may not pause to carefully evaluate statement 3, assuming Parliament's constituent power is unlimited.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Correct — the 44th Amendment inserted the proviso to Article 359(1) that explicitly excludes Articles 20 and 21 from any Presidential Order.
Verify Statement 2: Correct — the historical record confirms the 44th Amendment was Parliament's direct legislative response to ADM Jabalpur.

Verify Statement 3: Incorrect — no mechanism, including constitutional amendment, can authorise suspension of Articles 20 and 21 during emergency under the current framework; this is treated as non-negotiable.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the trap. Students with partial knowledge know that Parliament can amend the Constitution and may assume that even the 44th Amendment's safeguards could themselves be amended. However, the constitutional position — reinforced by the basic structure doctrine — is that Articles 20 and 21 represent a floor of rights that cannot be taken away, not even through emergency provisions. A student rushing through will mark 'all three' without scrutinising this nuance.
solution.final_explanation:
The 44th Amendment 1978 is one of India's most significant constitutional corrections, enacted after the excesses of the 1975-77 Emergency. Its core contribution in this area was making Articles 20 and 21 immune from Presidential Orders under Article 359.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 359(1), after the 44th Amendment, explicitly excludes Articles 20 and 21 from the scope of any Presidential Order — these rights remain fully enforceable even when emergency is in force.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The ADM Jabalpur case (1976) allowed courts to turn away Habeas Corpus petitions during emergency; the 44th Amendment constitutionally reversed this position.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The exclusion of Articles 20 and 21 is not merely statutory — it is embedded in the constitutional text as an absolute protection. Parliament cannot authorise their suspension through any route, including constitutional amendment, given basic structure constraints.

Value Addition:
• Justice H.R. Khanna's lone dissent in ADM Jabalpur that Article 21 could not be suspended was later described as one of India's finest judicial moments.
• The 44th Amendment also changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion' as an emergency ground.
• Justice D.Y. Chandrachud (Jr.) formally overruled ADM Jabalpur in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017).

solution.concept_anchor: Article 358 applies only to war or external aggression emergency

statement_analysis.statement: Article 358 automatically suspends Article 19 Fundamental Rights whenever a National Emergency is proclaimed under Article 352, regardless of the ground on which it is declared.
statement_analysis.reason: After the 44th Amendment 1978, Article 358 operates only when the emergency is proclaimed on the ground of war or external aggression — it does NOT apply when the ground is armed rebellion.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 358, any law enacted or executive action taken during the emergency period that abridges Article 19 rights is automatically valid, even if it has no connection with the emergency.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-44th Amendment, Article 358(1) requires that the law or executive action must have a nexus with the emergency — laws with no connection to the emergency cannot claim immunity under Article 358.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 358 suspends Article 19 Fundamental Rights for the duration of the emergency and not beyond.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 358 suspension of Article 19 operates only for the duration of the National Emergency; once the emergency ends, the suspension lapses (subject to the six-month survival clause for laws made during emergency).

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that Statement 1 is wrong (armed rebellion exclusion) may assume Statement 2 is correct because they recall that 'laws during emergency get immunity,' missing the post-44th Amendment nexus requirement.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Incorrect — the 44th Amendment restricted Article 358 to war/external aggression emergencies; armed rebellion does not trigger Article 358.
Evaluate Statement 2: Incorrect — the nexus requirement introduced by the 44th Amendment means a law must relate to the emergency to claim Article 358 immunity; blanket immunity no longer exists.
Evaluate Statement 3: Correct — Article 358 suspension is time-limited to the emergency period; this statement is accurate.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the common misconception that Article 358 applies to all three grounds of National Emergency. Before the 44th Amendment, this was arguably true, but post-amendment, only war/external aggression triggers automatic Article 19 suspension. Statement 2 exploits the assumption that all government actions during emergency get blanket protection — the nexus requirement corrected this. Students who studied the pre-amendment position or relied on older textbooks will be misled.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 358 is a targeted provision that automatically suspends Article 19 during National Emergency, but its scope was significantly narrowed by the 44th Amendment Act 1978.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 358 is triggered only by emergencies declared on the grounds of war or external aggression. A proclamation based on armed rebellion does NOT activate Article 358 — this is a critical 44th Amendment change.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The pre-amendment position allowed any law during emergency to override Article 19. The 44th Amendment introduced a nexus requirement — only laws and executive actions that are related to the emergency can claim immunity from Article 19 challenge.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The suspension under Article 358 is coterminous with the emergency; it does not extend beyond the proclamation period.

Value Addition:
• Before the 44th Amendment, the ground 'internal disturbance' could trigger Article 358; this was replaced by 'armed rebellion' and simultaneously excluded from Article 358's scope.
• Laws made under Article 358 immunity survive for six months after emergency ends — a key post-emergency accountability rule.
• Article 19 has six freedoms; all six are affected by Article 358 suspension.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 359 Presidential Order — mechanics and territorial scope

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential Order under Article 359 must specify which Fundamental Rights under Part III (other than Articles 20 and 21) are to be rendered unenforceable.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 359(1) requires the President to specify the rights in the order; it is not a blanket suspension — Articles 20 and 21 are explicitly excluded from such specification.

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential Order under Article 359 must extend to the whole territory of India and cannot be limited to a specified part.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 359(1A) provides that the Presidential Order may apply to the whole of India or to such part thereof as may be specified — territorial limitation is constitutionally permissible.

statement_analysis.statement: An order issued under Article 359 must be laid before each House of Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: The Constitution requires that every order made under Article 359 be laid before each House of Parliament — this is part of the parliamentary oversight mechanism.

statement_analysis.statement: Once issued, a Presidential Order under Article 359 can only be revoked by a resolution of Parliament and not by a subsequent Presidential Order.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 359(2) provides that the President may by order vary or revoke a previous order — revocation does not require a parliamentary resolution; it can be done by executive action.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students correctly identify statements 1 and 3 as true but may also accept statement 4 as true, believing (as with the emergency itself) that Parliament must be involved in revocation.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Correct — specificity is mandatory; Article 359(1) requires the order to name the rights.
Statement 2: Incorrect — territorial limitation of the order is permitted under Article 359(1A); 'whole India only' is false.
Statement 3: Correct — parliamentary laying is constitutionally required for Article 359 orders.
Statement 4: Incorrect — revocation can be done by a subsequent Presidential Order without requiring Parliament; only two statements (1 and 3) are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is designed to exploit confusion between the procedural requirements for revoking the emergency proclamation itself (which involves Parliament) and revoking a Presidential Order under Article 359 (which the President can do unilaterally). Students who conflate these two distinct procedures will over-count the correct statements. Statement 2 is a scope-extension trap — students assume territorial coverage must be all-India because the emergency itself is proclaimed for all or part of India.
solution.final_explanation:
A Presidential Order under Article 359 is the executive mechanism through which specific Fundamental Rights are rendered temporarily unenforceable. Understanding its mechanics precisely is essential.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Must specify which FRs are covered (excluding Arts. 20 & 21) | Correct |
| Must extend to whole India only | Incorrect |
| Must be laid before each House of Parliament | Correct |
| Can only be revoked by Parliament | Incorrect |

• Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (c).

Value Addition:
• Article 359 orders are distinct from Article 358 — the former is executive-initiated and specific; the latter is automatic and constitutional.
• The six-month post-emergency survival of laws applies to Article 358, not to Article 359 orders.
• A Presidential Order can be issued under Article 359 even before formal parliamentary approval of the emergency, though it lapses if the emergency itself is not approved.

solution.concept_anchor: ADM Jabalpur dissent and Puttaswamy overruling
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Justice H.R. Khanna dissented may not recall the precise pairing of which Justice Chandrachud dissented in ADM Jabalpur versus which overruled it, leading to entity-swap errors in column matching.
elimination_logic: Match A (ADM Jabalpur majority) with 3: The 4:1 majority held that during emergency, no locus standi exists to enforce Article 21 — this is the majority ruling, not a dissent.
Match B (Justice H.R. Khanna) with 1: His lone dissent arguing that Right to Life cannot be suspended is the defining constitutional moment of ADM Jabalpur.
Match C (44th Amendment 1978) with 4: The amendment constitutionally nullified ADM Jabalpur by making Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable.
Match D (K.S. Puttaswamy 2017) with 2: The Supreme Court in Puttaswamy expressly overruled ADM Jabalpur — this logical sequence confirms option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in confusing the two Chandrachuds. Justice D.Y. Chandrachud Sr. dissented in ADM Jabalpur, but it was Justice D.Y. Chandrachud Jr. who overruled it in Puttaswamy (2017). Students who recall 'a Chandrachud dissented in ADM Jabalpur' may incorrectly assign the Puttaswamy overruling to the same person or confuse the roles. Additionally, students may confuse Justice Khanna's dissent with the Puttaswamy judgment.
solution.final_explanation:
ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976) is one of India's most consequential — and controversial — constitutional cases. Understanding the cast of judicial actors and the subsequent legal history is critical.

• A–3 (Correct): The majority (4:1) in ADM Jabalpur held that during a Presidential Order under Article 359, courts have no jurisdiction to hear Habeas Corpus petitions for Article 21 enforcement — this was the majority position.
• B–1 (Correct): Justice H.R. Khanna authored the lone dissent, arguing that the right to life exists independent of any legal provision and cannot be taken away even during emergency — later described as an act of great judicial courage.
• C–4 (Correct): The 44th Amendment 1978 embedded the protection of Articles 20 and 21 in the constitutional text itself, removing any future executive or legislative ability to suspend them.
• D–2 (Correct): The nine-judge bench in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) expressly and unanimously overruled ADM Jabalpur — Justice D.Y. Chandrachud Jr. writing emphatically that the majority had 'wounded the Constitution.'

Value Addition:
• Justice H.R. Khanna was superseded for the Chief Justice position after his ADM Jabalpur dissent — widely seen as judicial victimization.
• The Shah Commission (1977) separately documented emergency-era excesses.
• The Puttaswamy case primarily dealt with the right to privacy but its overruling of ADM Jabalpur has lasting significance for emergency jurisprudence.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 358 not triggered by President's Rule or Financial Emergency
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who correctly know that A is true (Article 19 is not suspended during President's Rule) may incorrectly reject R, assuming some emergency-like condition applies during Article 356, leading them to mark (c).
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. Article 19 Fundamental Rights are NOT suspended during President's Rule under Article 356; only National Emergency under Article 352 triggers Article 358.
Step 2: Is R correct? — Yes. Article 358 is constitutionally confined to National Emergency proclaimed on grounds of war or external aggression — this is an accurate statement of law.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — No. The reason A is true is not merely because Article 358 is confined to war/external aggression emergencies — it is because Article 356 (President's Rule) is an entirely different constitutional provision that has no mechanism for FR suspension at all. R is a true statement about Article 358 but it does not causally explain why Article 19 survives during Article 356.
A is correct, R is correct, but R does NOT explain A — the correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question is designed to test whether students understand that a true reason may not be the causal explanation for a true assertion. R correctly describes a feature of Article 358 (it applies only to war/external aggression), but the real reason Article 19 is not suspended during President's Rule is that Article 356 is a completely different kind of constitutional provision — it governs state governance failure, not threats to national security, and has no FR-suspension mechanism whatsoever. Students who merely verify both statements as true and select (a) will lose the mark.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 358 and Article 356 operate in entirely separate constitutional domains. Article 358 is a creature of National Emergency (Article 352); Article 356 (President's Rule) governs a state's constitutional machinery failure.

• Assertion (A): Correct. Citizens in states under President's Rule retain all Fundamental Rights including Article 19 freedoms. No provision of the Constitution suspends FRs during President's Rule.
• Reason (R): Correct. Article 358's application is indeed confined to war and external aggression emergencies after the 44th Amendment — armed rebellion and certainly President's Rule do not trigger it.
• Causal relationship: Absent. The reason Article 19 is not suspended during President's Rule is not that Article 358 is limited to war/external aggression — it is that Article 356 is a structurally different provision with no FR-suspension mechanism. R is a true but unconnected fact.

The correct answer is (b): both A and R are correct, but R does not explain A.

Value Addition:
• Under President's Rule, Parliament legislates for the state but must still conform to FRs.
• Financial Emergency (Article 360) also has no mechanism for FR suspension.
• The distinction between Articles 352, 356, and 360 and their respective effects on FRs is a recurring UPSC theme.

solution.concept_anchor: Legislative milestones of emergency jurisprudence in chronological order
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the 42nd Amendment came before the 44th may incorrectly place the 38th Amendment later, or confuse the year of the ADM Jabalpur judgment with the 38th Amendment.
elimination_logic: Place ADM Jabalpur: The judgment was delivered in April 1976, during the Emergency period — this is the earliest event among the judicial/legislative responses.

Place 42nd Amendment: Enacted in 1976 (during the Emergency), it expanded emergency powers and made emergency proclamation partly non-justiciable — comes after ADM Jabalpur in the same year but enacted later.
Place 44th Amendment: Enacted in 1978 after the Emergency ended — it reversed 42nd Amendment excesses, changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion,' and protected Articles 20 and 21.

Place Puttaswamy: The nine-judge bench judgment was delivered in 2017 — the most recent event. Correct chronological order: ADM Jabalpur (1976) → 42nd Amendment (1976) → 44th Amendment (1978) → Puttaswamy (2017), which corresponds to option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the temporal proximity of ADM Jabalpur and the 42nd Amendment — both are from 1976. Students who know these are 'emergency era' events may reverse them or misplace the 38th Amendment. Additionally, some students confuse the 38th Amendment (1975, made emergency non-justiciable) with the 42nd Amendment (1976, which expanded it further). The correct sequence requires knowing that ADM Jabalpur was a judicial event preceding the 42nd Amendment's legislative consolidation of emergency powers.
solution.final_explanation:
The arc of emergency jurisprudence and legislation spans four decades and must be understood chronologically.

• ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976): The Supreme Court ruled 4:1 that Article 21 cannot be enforced during a Presidential Order under Article 359 — the starting point of this constitutional controversy.
• 42nd Amendment Act (1976): Enacted by the Indira Gandhi government during the Emergency; it expanded Article 352, restricted judicial review, and added the 'internal disturbance' provision more extensively.
• 44th Amendment Act (1978): The Janata government's corrective; changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion,' made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable, and introduced procedural safeguards.
• K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017): The nine-judge bench expressly overruled ADM Jabalpur, concluding that the majority had erred in permitting life and liberty to be suspended.

Correct sequence: ADM Jabalpur → 42nd Amendment → 44th Amendment → Puttaswamy — option (b).

Value Addition:
• The 38th Amendment (1975) made emergency proclamation non-justiciable — it was struck down in Minerva Mills (1980).
• The 44th Amendment required Cabinet advice in writing before emergency proclamation.
• Shah Commission (1977) documented emergency-era excesses in detail.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 226 High Court writ survives Article 359 suspension
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that a Presidential Order under Article 359 suspends the right to move courts will conclude that Priya has no judicial remedy, missing the crucial distinction that Article 226 High Court jurisdiction is not suspended by Article 359.
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable principle: Article 359 suspends the right to move courts under Article 32 (Supreme Court), not under Article 226 (High Court).
Eliminate (a): Priya is not without any remedy — Article 226 High Court jurisdiction survives an Article 359 Presidential Order.
Eliminate (b): The Presidential Order validly suspends Article 32 enforcement — her petition to the Supreme Court under Article 32 will not be entertainable.
Eliminate (d): Parliament would need to pass a separate law to restrict Article 226 — it has not happened automatically; Priya's High Court remedy survives.
Select (c): Priya can approach the High Court under Article 226 for a writ of Habeas Corpus even though her right to approach the Supreme Court under Article 32 is suspended.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The most common error is assuming that an Article 359 Presidential Order that suspends Article 32 enforcement also removes all judicial remedies. In reality, Article 226 (High Court writ jurisdiction) is a separate constitutional provision not directly covered by Article 359. Only a separate parliamentary law under Article 359(1A) can restrict High Court jurisdiction under Article 226 — and even then, the 44th Amendment background makes this deeply controversial. Students who think 'courts suspended means all courts' will choose (a).
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the critical distinction between Article 32 (Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction — itself a Fundamental Right) and Article 226 (High Court's writ jurisdiction — not a Fundamental Right but a constitutional power).

Applicable principle: Article 359 Presidential Orders can suspend the right to enforce specified FRs under Article 32. However, Article 226 — the High Court's writ jurisdiction — is not a Fundamental Right and therefore is not directly suspended by an Article 359 order. Parliament would need to pass a separate law to restrict it.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Priya retains the right to approach the High Court under Article 226 — she is not entirely without remedy.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Presidential Order legitimately suspends Article 32 enforcement for specified FRs; the Supreme Court will not entertain her Article 32 petition for the suspended right.
• Option (c) — Correct: Priya can file a Habeas Corpus petition in the High Court under Article 226, which remains operational.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Parliament has not automatically restricted Article 226 — a separate law is required; Priya's High Court remedy is intact.

Value Addition:
• Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right; Article 226 is not — this distinction determines their respective susceptibility to Article 359 orders.
• Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.
• Post-44th Amendment, since Article 21 cannot be suspended, Habeas Corpus petitions for Article 21 violations can be filed even under Article 32.

solution.concept_anchor: Only National Emergency triggers FR suspension mechanisms
solution.strong_distractor: d — Students may think President's Rule (Article 356) involves some FR suspension because governance is taken over by the Centre, making option (d) feel like an odd one out. In reality, it is Financial Emergency that most textbooks treat separately.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: constitutional provisions that DO NOT trigger automatic or Presidential Order-based suspension of any Fundamental Rights.
Article 356 (President's Rule): Does not suspend any FR — eliminate as fitting the category.
Article 360 (Financial Emergency): Does not suspend any FR — fits the category.
Article 352 on grounds of Armed Rebellion: Does not trigger Article 358 (Article 358 applies only to war/external aggression) — fits the category.
Article 352 on grounds of External Aggression: DOES trigger Article 358, automatically suspending Article 19 — this is the odd one out. Select (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the common student assumption that any National Emergency suspends Article 19. Armed rebellion (one of the three grounds under Article 352) does NOT trigger Article 358. Only war or external aggression does. Students who have not studied the 44th Amendment's refinement of Article 358 will treat all Article 352 proclamations as equivalent and incorrectly eliminate option (c) instead of (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The question tests whether students understand that not all emergencies lead to FR suspension, and not even all grounds of National Emergency trigger Article 358.

• Option (a) — Fits the category (does NOT suspend FRs): Article 356 (President's Rule) is a state-level constitutional breakdown provision. No Fundamental Right is suspended.
• Option (b) — Does NOT fit; this is the odd one out: National Emergency proclaimed on the ground of external aggression triggers Article 358, which automatically suspends Article 19. This is the only option in the list that actually leads to FR suspension.
• Option (c) — Fits the category: National Emergency proclaimed on the ground of armed rebellion does NOT trigger Article 358 — the 44th Amendment explicitly restricted Article 358 to war and external aggression.
• Option (d) — Fits the category: Financial Emergency (Article 360) has no mechanism for FR suspension whatsoever.

Value Addition:
• Article 360 has never been proclaimed in Indian history.
• Article 358 applies to all six freedoms under Article 19, not selectively.
• The 44th Amendment's exclusion of armed rebellion from Article 358's scope was a deliberate anti-misuse safeguard.

solution.concept_anchor: Suspension vs abridgement distinction — Article 359 effect

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 359, the Fundamental Rights specified in the Presidential Order are suspended for the duration of the emergency, meaning those rights temporarily cease to exist in law.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 359 does not suspend the Fundamental Right itself — it suspends the right to move courts for enforcement. The FR continues to exist in law but becomes unenforceable; this is a critical constitutional distinction.

statement_analysis.statement: Fundamental Rights cannot be waived by an individual citizen since they are conferred not merely for personal benefit but also in the public interest.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court in Behram Khurshid Pesikaka v. State of Bombay held that FRs cannot be waived by individuals as they serve a public purpose beyond individual interests — waiver doctrine applicable to ordinary rights does not apply.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who recall the general principle of FR non-waiveability (Statement 2) as correct may extend that correct instinct to accept Statement 1 without scrutinising whether 'suspension' under Article 359 means the right 'ceases to exist' — it does not.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Under Article 359, courts cannot enforce the specified FR, but the right itself continues to exist — it does not 'temporarily cease to exist in law.' Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: The Supreme Court's position in Behram Khurshid Pesikaka is precisely that FRs serve public interest and cannot be waived individually — Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 is incorrect; Statement 2 is correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The philosophical distinction in Statement 1 is the core trap. Students conflate 'unenforceability' with 'non-existence.' When Article 359 suspends the right to move courts, the FR continues to exist as a constitutional guarantee — it simply cannot be vindicated in court during that period. This is fundamentally different from the right ceasing to exist. The same distinction distinguishes Article 358 (which affects the validity of State action) from Article 359 (which affects the citizen's enforcement mechanism).
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the vocabulary of FR restriction is essential for constitutional law questions.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The precise language of Article 359 is that the right to move courts for enforcement is suspended, not the FR itself. The right 'exists' during the emergency — if the emergency ends or the order is revoked, it immediately becomes enforceable. This is why Article 359 is philosophically distinct from outright abolition.
• Statement 2 — Correct: In Behram Khurshid Pesikaka, the Supreme Court held that because FRs serve the public at large and not merely the individual holder, they cannot be waived. This distinguishes FRs from contractual rights or procedural rights that can be voluntarily surrendered.

Value Addition:
• Article 358 affects State action (laws abridging Article 19 become valid); Article 359 affects citizen enforcement rights.
• The distinction between suspension, abridgement, and waiver is frequently tested in UPSC Mains as well.
• In contrast, some procedural rights like the right to speedy trial have been treated as partially waivable in international jurisprudence, but not under Indian FR doctrine.

solution.concept_anchor: Six-month survival of emergency laws abridging Article 19
solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Immediately' feels correct to students who assume that once the emergency ends, the constitutional bar lifts immediately; the six-month grace period is a nuanced provision they may have missed.
elimination_logic: Recall Article 358(2): Laws made during a National Emergency that abridge Article 19 rights do not lapse immediately when the emergency ends.
The Constitution provides a six-month window during which such laws continue in force after the emergency ceases — this is the textually correct period.
Options naming 'three months' or 'one year' are temporal-swap distractors; 'immediately' is a scope-extension distractor.
The correct blank-filler is 'six months after the emergency ceases to operate' — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The six-month survival clause is a precise constitutional detail. Students who know that laws 'survive' after emergency ends but do not recall the exact period will guess between the options. The 'immediately' option is attractive to students who conflate the end of the emergency proclamation with the immediate restoration of all FR safeguards. The 'one year' option tempts those who over-remember the period.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 358(2) introduced a nuanced post-emergency accountability mechanism.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Three months is not the constitutionally specified period — this is a temporal-swap distractor.
• Option (b) — Correct: Laws made during the emergency that abridge Article 19 rights automatically become inoperative six months after the emergency ceases — this is the precise text of Article 358(2).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The suspension does not lift 'immediately' upon the emergency's end — the six-month grace period is specifically designed to allow legislative review and adjustment.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: One year is an over-extension; the correct period is six months.

Value Addition:
• The six-month rule applies to legislative actions; executive actions that violated Article 19 do not benefit from this grace period under Article 358(2).
• This provision ensures some continuity in emergency measures while requiring eventual legislative reaffirmation.
• Compare with Article 123: Ordinances lapse six weeks after Parliament reassembles — a similar 'grace period' logic.

solution.concept_anchor: Minerva Mills — judicial review of emergency proclamation
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may attribute the 'basic structure applies to emergency' holding to Kesavananda Bharati (1973), which established the basic structure doctrine, not Minerva Mills, which applied it specifically to emergency powers.
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) held that the 38th Amendment's attempt to make emergency proclamation non-justiciable was unconstitutional as judicial review is a basic feature — this pairing is correct.
Evaluate (b): Kesavananda Bharati established the basic structure doctrine but did not specifically rule on the justiciability of emergency proclamations — entity-swap distractor.
Evaluate (c): ADM Jabalpur addressed enforcement of rights during emergency, not the justiciability of the proclamation itself — the pairing with 'mala fide review' is fabricated.
Evaluate (d): Maneka Gandhi (1978) dealt with the right to travel and procedural due process under Article 21 — not emergency justiciability — this is a plausible-fabrication pairing.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap pairs Kesavananda Bharati with the emergency justiciability holding. Students who know that judicial review is a basic structure component and that Kesavananda Bharati established the basic structure doctrine will instinctively link the two, not realising that it was Minerva Mills that specifically applied this to strike down the 38th Amendment's attempt to remove emergency proclamations from judicial scrutiny.
solution.final_explanation:
The justiciability of emergency proclamations is a fundamental question of constitutional law.

• Option (a) — Correct: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck down the 38th Amendment (1975) which had declared emergency proclamations non-justiciable. The Supreme Court held judicial review to be a basic structure element — this pairing is perfectly matched.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) established the basic structure doctrine but did not specifically address emergency justiciability — entity-swap trap.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: ADM Jabalpur concerned the enforceability of Article 21 during a Presidential Order under Article 359, not the justiciability of the proclamation itself — partial-truth distractor.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) expanded the scope of Article 21's procedural protection — unrelated to emergency proclamation review.

Value Addition:
• The 38th Amendment (1975) was one of the most constitutionally aggressive amendments; Minerva Mills reversed its core effect.
• Courts apply a limited/subjective standard of review to Presidential 'satisfaction' — they check for mala fide or irrelevant material, not full merits review.
• The 44th Amendment also contributed procedural safeguards that complemented the Minerva Mills judicial position.

solution.concept_anchor: Preventive detention Article 22 and post-44th Amendment Article 21 protection

statement_analysis.statement: Article 22 explicitly authorises Parliament to enact preventive detention laws, and these laws can impose longer periods of detention during a National Emergency than what is ordinarily permissible.
statement_analysis.reason: Articles 22(4)-(7) establish the constitutional framework for preventive detention, and during National Emergency, Parliament's expanded legislative power allows more extensive preventive detention provisions than would normally pass muster under Article 22.

statement_analysis.statement: Even after the 44th Amendment 1978, a Presidential Order under Article 359 can abridge the procedural safeguards guaranteed under Article 22(1) and 22(2) against persons detained under preventive detention laws.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 22(1) and (2) apply to arrested persons, not those under preventive detention; more importantly, a Presidential Order under Article 359 can suspend enforcement of Article 22 rights, but it cannot touch Articles 20 or 21 — the statement wrongly implies the 44th Amendment created no bar on preventive detention-related Article 22 rights.

statement_analysis.statement: The MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act) was used during the 1975 Emergency in conjunction with a Presidential Order under Article 359 that had suspended enforcement of Articles 21 and 22.
statement_analysis.reason: During the 1975 Emergency, the Presidential Order under Article 359 specifically suspended the right to enforce Articles 21 and 22 — this was precisely what the 44th Amendment was designed to prevent from recurring for Article 21.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All three' is tempting because Statement 3 is correct and Statement 1 is correct; the error is in not carefully parsing Statement 2, which conflates preventive detention procedural rights with the 44th Amendment's scope.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Correct — Article 22(4)-(7) is the constitutional basis for preventive detention; emergency expands the permissible detention duration.

Verify Statement 2: Incorrect — Article 22(1) and (2) apply to accused persons, not preventees; and the statement's framing suggests the 44th Amendment created no bar, which is misleading regarding Article 21's protection.
Verify Statement 3: Correct — the 1975 Emergency Presidential Order suspending Articles 21 and 22 is historical fact; the 44th Amendment corrected this for Article 21.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Statement 2 is not — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is constructed as a partial-truth trap. The first part (Article 22 enforcement can be abridged by Article 359 order) is technically correct for Article 22 in isolation — since Article 22 is not Article 20 or 21, it can be specified in a Presidential Order. However, the statement is framed to suggest this is unaffected by the 44th Amendment, which is misleading because the Amendment specifically targeted Article 21 and created a broader constitutional culture of rights protection that constrains how Article 22 can be used in tandem with Article 21 claims.
solution.final_explanation:
Preventive detention sits at the intersection of Article 22 and emergency powers — a doubly sensitive constitutional zone.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Articles 22(4)-(7) provide the constitutional architecture for preventive detention. Parliament can enact laws allowing longer pre-advisory board review periods during emergency than the three-month ordinary limit.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The statement conflates two separate clusters — Article 22(1) and (2) relate to criminal arrest (right to be informed of grounds, right to a lawyer), not preventive detention. Moreover, the statement implies the 44th Amendment made no difference — but since Article 21 underlies the right to liberty in preventive detention, post-44th Amendment it cannot be suspended, limiting effective use of Article 359 in preventive detention contexts.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 1975 Emergency Presidential Order suspended enforcement of Articles 21 and 22 — this is the specific historical episode that the 44th Amendment was designed to prevent from recurring.

Value Addition:
• The advisory board requirement under Article 22(4) is a safeguard within preventive detention even during normal times.
• Parliament can extend preventive detention beyond three months only if an advisory board recommends it.
• MISA was repealed in 1977 by the Janata government; the National Security Act 1980 is the current preventive detention law.

solution.concept_anchor: Partial emergency territorial scope of Article 358 and 359

statement_analysis.statement: Following the 42nd Constitutional Amendment, a National Emergency can be proclaimed for a specified part of India's territory, and the effects of Articles 358 and 359 are correspondingly limited to that territory.
statement_analysis.reason: The 42nd Amendment enabled partial proclamation of emergency; the FR suspension effects under Articles 358 and 359 are also territorially limited to the part of India covered by the proclamation.

statement_analysis.statement: When a National Emergency is proclaimed for a part of India only, citizens in the areas NOT covered by the emergency continue to enjoy their Article 19 Fundamental Rights without any suspension.
statement_analysis.reason: Since Article 358 operates territorially in step with the emergency proclamation, citizens in non-emergency areas are unaffected — their Article 19 rights remain fully intact and enforceable.

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential Order under Article 359 must always apply uniformly to the entire territory of India and cannot be limited to a specific region even when the emergency itself is partial.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 359(1A) explicitly provides that the Presidential Order may apply to the whole of India or to such part thereof as may be specified — territorial limitation of the order is constitutionally permissible.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may think both statements 1 and 3 are wrong, correctly rejecting Statement 3 but mistakenly rejecting Statement 1 because they do not recall whether it was the 42nd or 44th Amendment that introduced partial emergency.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Correct — the 42nd Amendment introduced partial emergency; Articles 358 and 359 effects are territorially bounded.
Evaluate Statement 2: Correct — the territorial limitation of the proclamation protects Article 19 rights in non-covered areas.
Evaluate Statement 3: Incorrect — Article 359(1A) expressly allows the Presidential Order to be territorially limited; a blanket all-India requirement is constitutionally incorrect.
Only Statement 3 is NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is in Statement 3, which appears authoritative by invoking the gravity of a Presidential Order and the expectation that emergency powers are applied uniformly. Students who have not read Article 359(1A) carefully will assume that because the emergency proclamation is a national-level event, its enforcement mechanism must also be national. The 42nd Amendment's introduction of partial emergency and Article 359(1A)'s territorial flexibility are less-studied provisions that this question directly tests.
solution.final_explanation:
The territorial dimension of emergency powers is a relatively underemphasised but examinable aspect.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 42nd Amendment 1976 enabled the President to proclaim emergency for part of India. When such a partial emergency is declared, Articles 358 and 359 operate only within that territory.
• Statement 2 — Correct: This follows logically — citizens in areas not covered by the emergency proclamation retain their full Article 19 and other Fundamental Rights. The Constitution does not create a blanket nationwide effect when the emergency itself is geographically limited.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 359(1A) specifically provides that the Presidential Order under Article 359 may be limited to a specified part of India. There is no constitutional requirement that it must cover the entire country.

Value Addition:
• The 42nd Amendment introduced partial emergency but also centralised several other powers — many of its provisions were reversed by the 44th Amendment.
• Partial emergency creates an asymmetric rights situation within India — an important constitutional anomaly.
• The President can also vary or revoke Article 359 orders by a subsequent order — including adjusting the territorial scope.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 32 suspendable vs Article 226 not suspendable by Article 359

statement_analysis.statement: Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) is itself a Fundamental Right and can therefore be suspended by a Presidential Order under Article 359.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 32 is listed under Part III as a Fundamental Right; since it is not Article 20 or 21, it can be specified in a Presidential Order under Article 359 and rendered unenforceable.

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential Order under Article 359 automatically suspends the jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 to issue writs, including Habeas Corpus.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 226 is not a Fundamental Right — it is a constitutional power of High Courts. Article 359 affects only the right of citizens to move courts under specified FRs; a separate parliamentary law under Article 359(1A) is needed to restrict Article 226 jurisdiction.

statement_analysis.statement: Dr. Ambedkar described Article 32 as the 'heart and soul of the Constitution' — its suspension during emergency is therefore constitutionally extraordinary.
statement_analysis.reason: Ambedkar's characterisation of Article 32 as the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution is historically recorded in the Constituent Assembly Debates; its suspendability under Article 359 (unlike Articles 20 and 21) underscores the gravity of such a Presidential Order.

statement_analysis.statement: Post-44th Amendment, even if Article 32 is suspended under a Presidential Order, a citizen can still approach the Supreme Court to enforce Articles 20 and 21 since these cannot be suspended.
statement_analysis.reason: Because Articles 20 and 21 cannot be specified in any Presidential Order under Article 359, citizens retain the right to enforce them under Article 32 — the suspension of Article 32 enforcement cannot extend to Articles 20 and 21.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' tempts students who correctly assess statements 1, 3, and 4 but have not carefully distinguished between the automatic effect of Article 359 on Article 226 (which does not exist) and the need for a separate parliamentary law.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Correct — Article 32 is a FR not protected from suspension under Article 359.
Statement 2: Incorrect — Article 359 does not automatically suspend Article 226; only a separate parliamentary law can restrict High Court writ jurisdiction.
Statement 3: Correct — Ambedkar's 'heart and soul' description of Article 32 is on record; its suspendability is constitutionally extraordinary.

Statement 4: Correct — even with Article 32 suspended, enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 via Article 32 remains available since those cannot be excluded from enforcement; three statements (1, 3, 4) are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Wait — reviewing the elimination: Statements 1, 3, and 4 are correct; Statement 2 is incorrect. That means three statements are correct. The correct option is (c) — 'Only three.' Let me recheck: correct_option field shows 'd' (All four). This needs correction. Three statements are correct: 1, 3, 4. Statement 2 is incorrect. So the answer is 'Only three' = option (c).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 32 occupies a unique position — it is both a Fundamental Right and the primary vehicle for enforcing other Fundamental Rights at the Supreme Court level.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Article 32 is a FR suspendable under Article 359 | Correct |
| Article 359 automatically suspends Article 226 High Court jurisdiction | Incorrect |
| Ambedkar called Article 32 the heart and soul of the Constitution | Correct |
| Enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 via Article 32 survives despite suspension order | Correct |

• Three statements (1, 3, 4) are correct — option (c).

Value Addition:
• Article 226 gives High Courts broader writ jurisdiction (against any person/authority) compared to Article 32 (limited to FR enforcement against State).
• Parliament can restrict Article 226 during emergency under Article 359(1A) but must do so by law — it is not automatic.
• The interplay between Articles 32 and 226 during emergency is one of the most tested areas in UPSC Prelims.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 32 suspendable vs Article 226 not suspendable by Article 359

statement_analysis.statement: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right and can be suspended by a Presidential Order under Article 359.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 32 is a Part III Fundamental Right and is not excluded from Article 359's reach (only Articles 20 and 21 are excluded); a Presidential Order can make Article 32 unenforceable for specified FRs.

statement_analysis.statement: A Presidential Order under Article 359 automatically suspends the jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 to issue writs.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 226 is a constitutional power of High Courts, not a Fundamental Right — Article 359 does not reach it automatically; Parliament must enact a separate law under Article 359(1A) to restrict it.

statement_analysis.statement: Dr. Ambedkar described Article 32 as the 'heart and soul of the Constitution,' reflecting the extraordinary significance of its potential suspension during emergency.
statement_analysis.reason: Ambedkar's characterisation is on record in the Constituent Assembly Debates; the suspendability of Article 32 (while Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended) is a stark constitutional asymmetry.

statement_analysis.statement: Even when Article 32 enforcement is suspended, citizens can still petition the Supreme Court to enforce Articles 20 and 21 since those cannot be covered by any Presidential Order under Article 359.
statement_analysis.reason: The constitutional bar on including Articles 20 and 21 in a Presidential Order under Article 359 means enforcement of these rights via Article 32 remains available — the suspension cannot extend to them.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All four' is the strongest distractor because statements 1, 3, and 4 are all correct; only students who precisely know that Article 226 is not automatically affected by Article 359 will reject statement 2.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Correct — Article 32 can be suspended under Article 359; it is not protected like Articles 20 and 21.
Statement 2: Incorrect — Article 359 does not automatically suspend Article 226; a parliamentary law is needed for that.
Statement 3: Correct — Ambedkar's 'heart and soul' description is constitutional history.
Statement 4: Correct — enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 under Article 32 cannot be suspended by any Presidential Order; three statements are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the critical trap. The instinctive assumption is that if a Presidential Order suspends enforcement of Article 32 (the right to approach the Supreme Court), then all writ remedies including High Court writs under Article 226 are also gone. This is constitutionally incorrect. Article 226 is a power of the High Court, not a Fundamental Right, and therefore falls outside the scope of Article 359. Parliament must specifically legislate to restrict Article 226 jurisdiction — it does not happen automatically.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 32 and Article 226 together form the judicial enforcement architecture for Fundamental Rights, but they have importantly different constitutional statuses.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 32 is a Fundamental Right listed in Part III; since it is not Articles 20 or 21, it can be specified in a Presidential Order under Article 359 and its enforcement suspended.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 226 grants writ-issuing power to High Courts — it is a constitutional power, not a Fundamental Right. An Article 359 order cannot touch it; Parliament must pass a law under Article 359(1A) to restrict High Court jurisdiction.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Ambedkar's 'heart and soul' characterisation of Article 32 in the Constituent Assembly Debates makes its potential suspension under Article 359 a matter of grave constitutional consequence.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The exclusion of Articles 20 and 21 from any Presidential Order under Article 359 means these rights remain enforceable under Article 32 even when other Article 32 enforcement is suspended.

Value Addition:
• Article 226 has broader scope than Article 32 — it can issue writs against any person or authority, not just the State.
• The asymmetry between Articles 32 and 226 during emergency was one reason Habeas Corpus petitions shifted to High Courts after ADM Jabalpur.
• Post-44th Amendment, the practical importance of this distinction diminished for Article 21 claims since they cannot be suspended.

solution.concept_anchor: 44th Amendment changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion'
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the 42nd Amendment significantly altered emergency provisions may attribute the 'armed rebellion' change to it, not realising it was the 44th Amendment that replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion.'
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The 42nd Amendment (1976) expanded emergency powers; it did not replace 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' — that correction came later.
Eliminate (c): The 38th Amendment (1975) made emergency proclamation non-justiciable — it did not change the terminology of emergency grounds.
Eliminate (d): The 43rd Amendment restored certain judicial powers but did not specifically address emergency grounds terminology.
Confirm (b): The 44th Amendment 1978 replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' as a ground for National Emergency — raising the threshold for proclamation.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who know the 42nd Amendment was the 'emergency-expanding' amendment and the 44th Amendment was the 'corrective' amendment often attribute all changes to these amendments correctly in a general sense but fail on specifics. The replacement of 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' is specifically a 44th Amendment change — not 42nd. The 42nd Amendment actually made emergency easier to proclaim; it was the 44th that tightened the threshold.
solution.final_explanation:
The terminology used in Article 352 to describe the grounds for National Emergency has constitutional significance because it determines how easily emergency can be proclaimed.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 42nd Amendment (1976) expanded emergency powers — including enabling partial emergency and making proclamation easier — but did not change 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion.'
• Option (b) — Correct: The 44th Amendment 1978 replaced the term 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' as a ground for National Emergency, deliberately raising the threshold.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The 38th Amendment (1975) immunised emergency proclamations from judicial review — reversed by Minerva Mills — but had nothing to do with the terminology change.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The 43rd Amendment (1977) restored some fundamental rights curtailed by the 42nd Amendment but did not deal with emergency proclamation grounds.

Value Addition:
• 'Internal disturbance' was seen as dangerously vague — the 1975 Emergency was proclaimed on this ground.
• 'Armed rebellion' requires active and organised violent resistance against the State — a much higher threshold.
• The 44th Amendment also required Cabinet advice in writing and Lok Sabha approval by special majority within one month.

solution.concept_anchor: FR obligations of State continue during emergency except where specifically suspended

statement_analysis.statement: During a National Emergency, State Governments retain the power to independently abridge Fundamental Rights of citizens without any authorisation from Parliament or a Presidential Order.
statement_analysis.reason: States cannot independently abridge Fundamental Rights during emergency — they can only do so if authorised by Parliamentary legislation or a Presidential direction. The suspension of FRs during emergency is a Union-level action, not a State prerogative.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 13, which declares laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights to be void, continues to operate during a National Emergency except where Articles 358 or 359 create specific exceptions.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 13's supremacy of FRs over ordinary law continues during emergency; it is only in the areas covered by Article 358 (Article 19 suspension during external aggression emergency) or Article 359 (Presidential Order on specified FRs) that the Article 13 bar is temporarily lifted.

statement_analysis.statement: During a National Emergency, Parliament can give directions to States under Article 353 but State action taken pursuant to such directions must still conform to Fundamental Rights not suspended by Articles 358 or 359.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliamentary supremacy during emergency under Article 353 does not override FR protections that remain in force — State actions implementing Parliamentary directions must still respect unsuspended FRs.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All three' traps students who correctly assess 2 and 3 but do not notice that Statement 1 grants State governments an independent power to abridge FRs, which they do not have.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Incorrect — States have no independent power to abridge FRs during emergency; Parliamentary legislation or Presidential direction is required.
Verify Statement 2: Correct — Article 13 continues in force; only Articles 358 and 359 create specific exceptions to it.
Verify Statement 3: Correct — Parliamentary directions to States under Article 353 do not override intact FR protections.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the common (and wrong) assumption that during emergency, all governmental actors — including State governments — get expanded powers to restrict civil liberties. In reality, the suspension of FRs flows only from central-level mechanisms (Presidential Orders, Parliamentary legislation). States remain bound by FRs that are not suspended, and cannot independently abridge them. This is a scope-extension error — 'emergency suspends FRs' is extended wrongly to mean 'all governments can abridge FRs.'
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between emergency powers and State obligations regarding Fundamental Rights is frequently misunderstood.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: State Governments cannot independently abridge any Fundamental Right during emergency — the power to suspend FRs vests at the Union level through Presidential Orders and Parliamentary legislation. States act under Parliamentary supremacy during emergency, not above it.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 13 (which voids FR-violating laws) continues to operate during emergency. The only exceptions are the zones carved out by Article 358 (external aggression emergency + Article 19) and Article 359 (Presidential Order specifying FRs). Every other FR retains Article 13 protection.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Parliamentary directions under Article 353 do not exempt State action from compliance with non-suspended Fundamental Rights. Emergency expands Parliament's power but does not reduce citizens' unsuspended FR entitlements.

Value Addition:
• Article 353 allows Parliament to extend its laws to State List subjects and give directions to States during emergency.
• Article 13(2) makes State action void if it infringes FRs — this applies to State actions during emergency for unsuspended FRs.
• UPSC often tests whether emergency creates a 'rights-free zone' — it does not; only specified FRs are affected.

solution.concept_anchor: ICCPR Article 4 mirrors India's post-44th Amendment position on right to life
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both facts may assume R explains A — India's post-44th Amendment position looks similar to ICCPR Article 4, which may lead students to assume the ICCPR influenced the amendment when in fact the 44th Amendment was driven by domestic constitutional concerns.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. India's position after the 44th Amendment 1978 (Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable) mirrors the ICCPR Article 4 position that the right to life cannot be derogated even during public emergency.

Step 2: Is R correct? — No. The 44th Amendment was enacted primarily as a domestic constitutional response to the ADM Jabalpur judgment and the 1975 Emergency excesses — not as an implementation of ICCPR commitments. India ratified the ICCPR in 1979, after the 44th Amendment was passed in 1978.
Step 3: Causation — moot since R is factually incorrect.
A is correct, R is incorrect — select option (c).
solution.final_explanation:
The comparison between India's emergency framework and international human rights law is a nuanced area.

• Assertion (A): Correct. After the 44th Amendment 1978, Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during National Emergency — this mirrors Article 4 of the ICCPR, which prohibits derogation from the right to life and freedom from torture even during public emergency. The substantive position is similar.
• Reason (R): Incorrect. The 44th Amendment was a domestic constitutional correction driven by the ADM Jabalpur judgment (1976) and the documented excesses of the 1975-77 Emergency. Critically, India ratified the ICCPR only in 1979 — one year after the 44th Amendment was enacted in 1978. The amendment could not have been enacted to comply with a treaty India had not yet ratified.

The correct answer is (c): A is correct but R is incorrect.

Value Addition:
• India ratified both the ICCPR and ICESCR in 1979.
• ICCPR Article 4 lists non-derogable rights including right to life, freedom from torture, and freedom of thought.
• Unlike India's written constitutional emergency framework, the UK relies on parliamentary sovereignty and the Human Rights Act for emergency powers — no codified FR suspension mechanism exists.

solution.concept_anchor: Six-month rule applies to laws not executive actions under Article 358

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 358(2), laws enacted during a National Emergency that abridged Article 19 rights automatically cease to operate six months after the emergency ends, but executive actions taken during the emergency under Article 358 immunity do not receive this six-month grace period.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 358(2) specifically mentions 'laws' in this context — executive actions that violated Article 19 during the emergency do not benefit from the six-month survival clause and can be challenged once the emergency ends without any grace period.

statement_analysis.statement: The six-month survival clause under Article 358(2) applies equally to laws enacted by Parliament and laws enacted by State Legislatures during the emergency period that abridged Article 19 rights.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 358(2) does not distinguish between Parliamentary and State Legislative laws — both categories of laws that abridged Article 19 under Article 358 immunity survive for six months after the emergency ends before becoming void.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the six-month rule applies to laws may assume it cannot apply equally to State Legislature laws — they may think only Parliamentary laws survive the six months, making Statement 2 appear incorrect.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Correct — the six-month grace period under Article 358(2) applies to laws, not to executive actions; executive actions can be challenged immediately after the emergency ends.
Evaluate Statement 2: Correct — Article 358(2) covers both parliamentary and state legislative laws without distinction; both survive six months after emergency.
Both statements are correct — select option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 358(2) introduces a critical post-emergency accountability rule that distinguishes between legislative and executive actions and also applies uniformly across legislative levels.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The six-month survival clause explicitly covers 'laws' — laws that abridged Article 19 continue in force for six months after the emergency so that the legislature has time to review them. Executive actions (government orders, administrative decisions) taken during emergency under Article 358 immunity cannot claim this grace period — they can be immediately challenged after emergency ends.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 358(2) does not limit the six-month rule to Parliamentary legislation alone. State Legislature laws enacted during the emergency that abridged Article 19 rights under the emergency's legislative framework also get the same six-month survival window.

Both statements are correct — option (a).

Value Addition:
• This distinction between laws and executive actions is a classic UPSC-precision trap — learn it carefully.
• The Shah Commission (1977) documented emergency-era executive actions that caused rights violations — the lack of post-emergency immunity for such actions was relevant to accountability proceedings.
• After six months, Article 19 freedoms resume full protection and any surviving emergency legislation becomes subject to normal FR scrutiny.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 358(2), laws enacted during a National Emergency that abridged Article 19 rights automatically cease to operate six months after the emergency ends, but executive actions taken during the emergency that violated Article 19 do not benefit from this six-month grace period.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 358(2) specifically applies to laws — executive actions have no constitutionally prescribed grace period and can be challenged immediately after the emergency ceases.

statement_analysis.reason: Article 358(2) draws no distinction between Parliamentary and State Legislature laws — both categories of Article 19-abridging legislation survive for six months after the emergency ends.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may think the six-month rule cannot apply to State Legislature laws since the emergency itself is a Union-level event, making Statement 2 appear incorrect to them.

solution.final_explanation:
Article 358(2) is a carefully calibrated post-emergency provision that balances administrative continuity with constitutional restoration.

• Statement 1 — Correct: 'Laws' that abridged Article 19 under emergency's Article 358 immunity survive for six months after the emergency ceases. Both statements are correct — option (a).

Value Addition:
• The six-month rule prevents administrative chaos by allowing a transition period for emergency-era legislation.
• Executive actions have no such protection — a deliberate constitutional design choice to create stronger accountability for executive overreach.
• Shah Commission (1977) findings highlighted how executive actions during 1975-77 Emergency caused disproportionate harm — the lack of post-emergency immunity for such actions reflects this constitutional learning.

solution.concept_anchor: Abridgement vs suspension vs waiver — distinct FR restriction concepts
solution.strong_distractor: a — 'Suspension' is the most familiar vocabulary in emergency discussions and students will instinctively choose it, not realising that reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2)-(6) constitute 'abridgement,' not 'suspension.'
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a) 'suspension': Suspension is a time-bound non-enforceability during emergency — it is not what Article 19(2)-(6) restrictions represent.

Eliminate (b) 'waiver': Waiver implies voluntary relinquishment by the rights-holder — the Supreme Court has held FRs cannot be waived by individuals; restrictions under Articles 19(2)-(6) are State-imposed, not individual waivers.
Eliminate (d) 'abrogation': Abrogation implies permanent removal — reasonable restrictions do not permanently remove the right.

Confirm (c) 'abridgement': Reasonable restrictions under Articles 19(2)-(6) are regulatory limitations that narrow the scope of exercise of Article 19 rights — this is constitutional abridgement, not suspension, waiver, or abrogation.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The term 'suspension' dominates discussions of emergency and FR restriction, so students conflate all FR restrictions with 'suspension.' The vocabulary distinction is precise: abridgement is a permanent (or ongoing) regulatory narrowing of a right; suspension is a temporary, emergency-context non-enforceability; waiver is voluntary relinquishment; abrogation is permanent abolition. Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2)-(6) belong strictly to the 'abridgement' category.
solution.final_explanation:
The vocabulary of Fundamental Rights restriction has constitutional precision that UPSC tests.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: 'Suspension' refers to the emergency-context temporary non-enforceability of FRs — not to the regulatory restrictions under Article 19(2)-(6) which operate in normal times.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 'Waiver' refers to voluntary relinquishment by the individual; the Supreme Court in Behram Khurshid Pesikaka held FRs cannot be waived since they serve public interest.
• Option (c) — Correct: 'Abridgement' is the precise term for reasonable restrictions imposed by the State on FR exercise — Articles 19(2)-(6) authorise legislative abridgement of Article 19 freedoms on specified grounds like security, public order, and morality.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 'Abrogation' means permanent abolition of a right — reasonable restrictions do not abolish the right; they regulate its exercise.

Value Addition:
• Article 13 uses 'abridges' to describe what laws cannot do to FRs — confirming that abridgement is the correct category.
• The suspension-abridgement distinction is central to understanding why Article 358 (which enables abridging laws during emergency) and Article 359 (which suspends enforcement) operate differently.
• Reasonable restrictions must satisfy the test of proportionality — expanded in Puttaswamy (2017).

solution.concept_anchor: Articles 358 and 359 — functional distinctions matched to features
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Article 359 requires a Presidential Order may correctly pair C-3 but then confuse A and B, mixing up which article applies to which ground of emergency or which article applies to Article 19 specifically.
elimination_logic: Match A (Article 358) with 2: Article 358 automatically suspends Article 19 — no Presidential Order required; it is self-executing upon emergency proclamation.
Match B (Article 359) with 4: Article 359 requires the President to issue an order specifying the FRs whose enforcement is suspended — it is not automatic.
Match C (Grounds triggering Article 358) with 1: Article 358 operates only when emergency is on grounds of war or external aggression — NOT armed rebellion.
Match D (FRs excluded from Article 359) with 3: Articles 20 and 21 are explicitly excluded — no Presidential Order can specify them; confirms option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The key entity-swap trap is between Articles 358 and 359. Students who know 'Article 358 suspends Article 19 automatically' may correctly identify A-2 but then swap B and D, thinking Article 359 applies to Article 19 or that Article 359 can apply to Articles 20 and 21. The exclusion of Articles 20 and 21 from Article 359 and the restriction of Article 358 to war/external aggression are the two most tested nuances in this pair.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 358 and 359 are the two mechanisms of FR suspension during National Emergency, and their differences are constitutionally significant.

• A–2 (Correct): Article 358 is the provision that automatically suspends Article 19 Fundamental Rights upon proclamation of National Emergency — no further Presidential action is needed.
• B–4 (Correct): Article 359 operates differently — the President must issue a specific order naming the FRs whose enforcement is to be suspended; it is not self-executing.
• C–1 (Correct): Article 358 is activated only by emergencies declared on grounds of war or external aggression. Armed rebellion — while a valid ground for National Emergency under Article 352 — does NOT trigger Article 358.
• D–3 (Correct): Articles 20 (protection against arbitrary conviction) and 21 (right to life and personal liberty) are the only FRs that cannot be specified in any Presidential Order under Article 359 — a constitutional floor introduced by the 44th Amendment.

Value Addition:
• Article 358 affects the validity of State action (laws abridging Article 19 become valid); Article 359 affects citizen enforcement rights.
• Article 359 suspension can be territorially limited; Article 358 operates uniformly where the emergency is proclaimed.
• The 44th Amendment's exclusion of Articles 20 and 21 from Article 359 is the constitutional legacy of ADM Jabalpur.

solution.concept_anchor: Only National Emergency leads to FR suspension — not Article 356 or 360
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who confuse President's Rule with some form of rights restriction because the Centre 'takes over' the State may select (b), assuming FR suspension accompanies the constitutional takeover.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Financial Emergency (Article 360) has never been proclaimed and has no FR suspension mechanism — neither Articles 358 nor 359 is triggered.
Eliminate (b): President's Rule (Article 356) is a state governance failure provision — no Fundamental Right is suspended; Article 19 remains fully operative.

Eliminate (c): National Emergency proclaimed for armed rebellion triggers Article 352 but does NOT activate Article 358 — Article 358's automatic Article 19 suspension applies only to war/external aggression.
Confirm (d): National Emergency on grounds of external aggression triggers Article 358, which automatically suspends Article 19 — this is the only option that correctly triggers FR suspension.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the widespread conflation of 'emergency' with 'FR suspension.' Students learn three types of emergency and assume all three affect FRs. In reality: Article 360 has no FR suspension mechanism; Article 356 has no FR suspension mechanism; even within Article 352, only war/external aggression triggers Article 358. The armed rebellion ground (option c) is a particularly effective trap because it IS a National Emergency ground but still does not activate Article 358.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between emergency types and FR suspension must be precisely mapped.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Financial Emergency (Article 360) empowers the President to direct states on financial matters and reduce salaries of officials and judges — it has no provision for FR suspension and has never been proclaimed.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: President's Rule (Article 356) is invoked when a state's constitutional machinery breaks down. Citizens retain all Fundamental Rights including Article 19 during President's Rule — a fundamental misconception to avoid.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Although armed rebellion is a valid ground for National Emergency under Article 352 after the 44th Amendment, it does NOT trigger Article 358. The Article 19 suspension under Article 358 is restricted to war and external aggression emergencies.
• Option (d) — Correct: National Emergency proclaimed on grounds of external aggression is the precise trigger for Article 358, which automatically suspends Article 19 rights for the duration of the emergency.

Value Addition:
• India has experienced National Emergency three times: 1962 (China War), 1971 (Pakistan War), and 1975 (internal disturbance).
• Only the 1975 Emergency involved a Presidential Order under Article 359 suspending Article 21 enforcement.
• Article 360 (Financial Emergency) has zero proclamation history in India.
