solution.concept_anchor: ADM Jabalpur majority holding and Justice Khanna dissent

statement_analysis.statement: In ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla, the Supreme Court's majority (4:1) held that during a Presidential Order under Article 359 suspending enforcement of Article 21, no person has locus standi to approach any court for enforcement of that right.
statement_analysis.reason: The majority judgment (Beg, Chandrachud, Bhagwati, and Ray JJ.) held that the right to approach courts for Article 21 enforcement was suspended and no writ of Habeas Corpus could be entertained — this was the core holding of the case.

statement_analysis.statement: Justice H.R. Khanna, in his dissent in ADM Jabalpur, argued that the right to life exists as a natural right independent of any statutory provision and cannot be abridged even by a Presidential Order under Article 359.
statement_analysis.reason: Justice Khanna's dissent rested on the philosophical position that the right to life predates and transcends any specific constitutional provision — it is inherent in personhood and cannot be suspended by any executive order.

statement_analysis.statement: The ADM Jabalpur judgment was expressly overruled in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) on the ground that Right to Life is a basic structure element.
statement_analysis.reason: ADM Jabalpur was decided in 1976 — it could not have been overruled by Kesavananda Bharati (1973), which preceded it by three years. ADM Jabalpur was formally overruled by K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017).

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All three' is tempting because students who know statements 1 and 2 are correct may not pause to check the chronology trap in Statement 3 — the claim that Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled a case decided in 1976 is chronologically impossible.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Correct — the 4:1 majority holding in ADM Jabalpur on locus standi is accurately described.
Verify Statement 2: Correct — Justice Khanna's natural rights argument in his dissent is historical fact.

Verify Statement 3: Incorrect — Kesavananda Bharati (1973) was decided three years before ADM Jabalpur (1976); a 1973 case cannot overrule a 1976 case. ADM Jabalpur was overruled by Puttaswamy (2017).
Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 contains a chronological impossibility that many students will miss if they focus on the substantive claim (basic structure + right to life) without checking the dates. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) is associated with the basic structure doctrine and is frequently linked to right-to-life arguments, making the statement seem plausible. However, ADM Jabalpur was decided in 1976 — three years after Kesavananda. Only Puttaswamy (2017) formally overruled ADM Jabalpur. This is a temporal-swap trap embedded in an entity-swap construction.
solution.final_explanation:
ADM Jabalpur is one of India's most studied and criticised constitutional judgments — understanding its precise holdings, dissents, and overruling is essential.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The four-judge majority (Chief Justice Ray, and Justices Beg, Chandrachud Sr., and Bhagwati) held that when a Presidential Order under Article 359 suspends enforcement of Article 21, no court has jurisdiction to issue Habeas Corpus for its enforcement. The right to approach courts was itself suspended.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Justice H.R. Khanna's lone dissent is constitutionally celebrated. He argued that the right to life is not merely a statutory or constitutional grant — it exists as a natural right inherent in humanity, which no executive order can suspend.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: This statement contains a temporal impossibility — Kesavananda Bharati was decided on April 24, 1973, whereas ADM Jabalpur was decided on April 28, 1976. A judgment cannot be overruled by an earlier case. ADM Jabalpur was formally and expressly overruled in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017).

Value Addition:
• Justice Khanna was subsequently superseded for the position of Chief Justice of India — widely interpreted as judicial victimisation.
• Justice D.Y. Chandrachud Jr. (son of Justice D.Y. Chandrachud Sr. who was in the ADM Jabalpur majority) wrote the most pointed critique of ADM Jabalpur in Puttaswamy.
• The 44th Amendment 1978 constitutionally nullified ADM Jabalpur's practical effect before the case was judicially overruled in 2017.

solution.concept_anchor: Judicial review of Presidential satisfaction — limited standard not full merits
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that courts can review emergency proclamations (Minerva Mills) may over-extend this to conclude that courts can examine the full merits of whether the security threat was real — they cannot; the standard is limited to mala fide or irrelevant grounds.
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable principle: Minerva Mills (1980) established that judicial review of emergency proclamation is possible but the standard is limited — courts can examine mala fide or whether the President's satisfaction was based on irrelevant material, not full merits.
Eliminate (a): Courts cannot review the 'adequacy' or 'sufficiency' of the material — this would be full merits review, which is beyond the limited standard applied to Presidential satisfaction.
Eliminate (b): Courts can entertain the challenge — the 38th Amendment's attempt to immunise proclamations from review was struck down in Minerva Mills.
Eliminate (d): The court need not wait for Parliament to revoke — it has jurisdiction to hear and decide the petition.

Select (c): The correct principle is that courts can review the proclamation for mala fide or use of irrelevant material, but cannot substitute their own judgment on whether the emergency was necessary.
solution.final_explanation:
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) is the foundational case on judicial review of emergency proclamations and represents the correct constitutional balance.

Applicable principle: The Supreme Court holds jurisdiction to examine emergency proclamations, but applies a limited standard of review — it can check whether the President's satisfaction was exercised in good faith (bona fide), whether relevant material existed, and whether irrelevant considerations influenced the proclamation. It cannot assess whether the material was 'adequate' or whether the threat was 'serious enough' — that would substitute the court's judgment for the President's.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Courts cannot examine whether the material was adequate or sufficient — this is full merits review, which is not the standard applied under limited review of Presidential satisfaction.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Courts can entertain the petition — the 38th Amendment's attempt to make proclamation non-justiciable was struck down in Minerva Mills; courts have jurisdiction.
• Option (c) — Correct: The court will examine whether the proclamation was issued in good faith based on relevant material — mala fide challenge is squarely within the limited review standard.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The court does not need to await Parliamentary action; it has concurrent jurisdiction to hear constitutional challenges.

Value Addition:
• The limited review standard balances executive primacy in national security with constitutional accountability.
• The 38th Amendment (1975) that tried to make emergency non-justiciable was struck down in Minerva Mills (1980).
• S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) applied similar limited review to Article 356 proclamations.

solution.concept_anchor: Habeas Corpus availability post-44th Amendment during emergency
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who associate Habeas Corpus with Article 32 (the original ADM Jabalpur context) may conclude that since Article 32 can be suspended, Habeas Corpus is also suspended — missing that Article 226 remains and that Article 21 post-44th Amendment cannot be suspended.
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): Habeas Corpus is available under both Articles 32 and 226 — not only under Article 32; and post-44th Amendment, since Article 21 cannot be suspended, even Article 32 Habeas Corpus is available for Article 21 violations. The pairing is incorrect.

Evaluate (b): Post-44th Amendment, since Article 21 (which underlies Habeas Corpus) cannot be specified in any Presidential Order under Article 359, Habeas Corpus petitions for Article 21 violations remain maintainable under Article 32 even during a Presidential Order — this pairing is correctly matched.

Evaluate (c): Habeas Corpus under Article 226 is available regardless of Article 359 orders since Article 226 is not a Fundamental Right — it cannot be suspended by Article 359 automatically; a separate parliamentary law is needed.
Evaluate (d): The Shah Commission investigated executive excesses during the 1975-77 Emergency but is not paired with Habeas Corpus availability — this is a plausible but fabricated pairing.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in option (a) is the incorrect assumption that Habeas Corpus is exclusively an Article 32 remedy. Pre-44th Amendment, ADM Jabalpur specifically blocked Habeas Corpus under Article 32 when Article 21 was suspended. But post-44th Amendment, since Article 21 cannot be suspended, the Article 32 avenue for Habeas Corpus is restored for Article 21 violations. Additionally, Article 226 was never suspended by the Article 359 order — another avenue students miss.
solution.final_explanation:
The availability of Habeas Corpus during emergency is one of the most tested questions in this sub-topic.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The statement that Habeas Corpus is available 'only through Article 226 High Courts' is wrong on two counts: first, post-44th Amendment, Article 21 cannot be suspended, so Habeas Corpus under Article 32 for Article 21 violations is also available; second, the 'only through' language is exclusionary and incorrect.
• Option (b) — Correct: After the 44th Amendment, since no Presidential Order under Article 359 can specify Articles 20 or 21, the right to enforce Article 21 through Article 32 remains intact. Habeas Corpus petitions for Article 21 violations are therefore maintainable under Article 32 even during a Presidential Order.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: While it is true that Article 226 cannot be suspended by an Article 359 order automatically, the claim that 'Parliament has no power to restrict Article 226 during emergency' is wrong — Parliament can restrict it by law under Article 359(1A).
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Shah Commission (1977) documented emergency-era excesses but it is not paired with Habeas Corpus availability as a constitutional rule.

Value Addition:
• ADM Jabalpur's core harm was blocking Habeas Corpus; the 44th Amendment restored this protection for Article 21.
• High Courts can hear Habeas Corpus under Article 226 even when Article 32 is partially suspended — a critical structural protection.
• The right to Habeas Corpus is so fundamental that even the ICCPR lists it as non-derogable.

solution.concept_anchor: 44th Amendment procedural safeguards for emergency proclamation

statement_analysis.statement: The 44th Amendment Act 1978 requires that a resolution approving the proclamation of National Emergency must be passed by both Houses of Parliament within one month by a simple majority of the total membership of the House.
statement_analysis.reason: The 44th Amendment requires approval by both Houses by a special majority — a majority of the total membership of the House AND a majority of not less than two-thirds of members present and voting — not a simple majority. This is one of the most-tested procedural details.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the 44th Amendment, a proclamation of National Emergency cannot be made on the basis of an imminent threat of war or external aggression — actual war or aggression must have already occurred.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 352 specifically retains the power to proclaim emergency when the President is satisfied that there is imminent danger of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion — actual occurrence is not a prerequisite. The 44th Amendment did not remove this forward-looking power.

statement_analysis.statement: The 44th Amendment introduced a safeguard under which the Lok Sabha can pass a resolution by simple majority to disapprove the continuation of a National Emergency, upon which the President must revoke it.
statement_analysis.reason: The 44th Amendment inserted a provision under which a special sitting of the Lok Sabha can be requisitioned by not less than one-tenth of its total membership, and if the Lok Sabha passes a resolution by a simple majority disapproving the emergency, the President must revoke it — this is the one instance in emergency law where a simple majority of one House is effective.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Statement 1 sounds plausible because students know approval requires a 'majority' and confuse whether it is simple or special; selecting 'only Statement 1' as incorrect misses that Statement 2 is also incorrect.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Incorrect — approval of emergency requires special majority (total membership majority + two-thirds of members present and voting), not simple majority.
Evaluate Statement 2: Incorrect — Article 352 allows proclamation on imminent danger, not just after actual occurrence; the 44th Amendment preserved this forward-looking power.
Evaluate Statement 3: Correct — the Lok Sabha revocation mechanism by simple majority is a 44th Amendment safeguard; this statement is accurate.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a classic partial-truth trap — the word 'simple majority' is the single error in an otherwise accurate description of the procedural requirement. The 44th Amendment raised the approval bar specifically to prevent emergency from being steamrolled through Parliament by a bare majority. Statement 2 exploits the assumption that tightening emergency thresholds (which the 44th Amendment did in other ways) also removed the 'imminent danger' provision — it did not.
solution.final_explanation:
The 44th Amendment introduced multiple procedural safeguards for National Emergency that require precise recall.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Parliamentary approval of emergency proclamation requires a 'special majority' — meaning a majority of the total membership of each House AND not less than two-thirds of members present and voting. 'Simple majority' is the critical error in this statement.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 352 specifically allows proclamation on grounds of 'imminent danger' of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion — actual occurrence is not required. The 44th Amendment tightened the process but preserved the forward-looking power.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 44th Amendment introduced the mechanism for Lok Sabha to pass a resolution disapproving the emergency by a simple majority, upon which the President must revoke the proclamation. Notably, this is one context where a simple majority of a single House — Lok Sabha — has decisive effect.

Value Addition:
• Special majority for emergency approval: total membership majority + two-thirds of members present and voting.
• Rajya Sabha resolution alone cannot force revocation — it is a Lok Sabha prerogative under the 44th Amendment.
• The Cabinet must advise the President in writing before emergency is proclaimed — another 44th Amendment safeguard.

solution.concept_anchor: Six freedoms under Article 19 — all suspended under Article 358
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may think the right to freedom of speech is the 'odd one out' because it is the most politically sensitive right and they may assume some distinction exists in how it is treated under Article 358, when in fact all six Article 19 freedoms are treated identically.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: rights guaranteed under Article 19 that are suspended under Article 358 during National Emergency on grounds of external aggression.
Right to freedom of speech and expression (Article 19(1)(a)): Part of Article 19 — suspended under Article 358.
Right to assemble peacefully without arms (Article 19(1)(b)): Part of Article 19 — suspended under Article 358.
Right to move freely throughout India (Article 19(1)(d)): Part of Article 19 — suspended under Article 358.

Right against self-incrimination (Article 20(3)): Part of Article 20, NOT Article 19 — Article 20 cannot be suspended even by Article 359; it is certainly not an Article 19 right. This is the odd one out — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the conflation of Articles 19 and 20. Article 20(3) (protection against self-incrimination) is listed under Article 20, not Article 19. Article 358 only suspends Article 19 rights. Moreover, Article 20 cannot be suspended even under Article 359. A student who has not carefully distinguished between which freedoms are in Article 19 versus Article 20 will fail to identify option (d) as the odd one out.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 19 guarantees six specific freedoms; Article 358 suspends all of them during external aggression emergencies. Article 20 is a separate provision protecting rights related to criminal proceedings.

• Option (a) — Part of Article 19: Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is one of the six Article 19 freedoms — it falls within the scope of Article 358 suspension.
• Option (b) — Part of Article 19: Right to assemble peacefully without arms under Article 19(1)(b) is an Article 19 freedom — suspended under Article 358.
• Option (c) — Part of Article 19: Right to move freely throughout India under Article 19(1)(d) is an Article 19 freedom — suspended under Article 358.
• Option (d) — NOT part of Article 19; this is the odd one out: Protection against self-incrimination is guaranteed under Article 20(3), not Article 19. Article 20 cannot be suspended by any Presidential Order under Article 359 and is not subject to Article 358.

Value Addition:
• The six Article 19 freedoms: speech/expression; assembly; association; movement; residence; profession/occupation/trade/business.
• Article 19(1)(c) — right to form associations — was removed from Article 19(1) in one version of the Constitution; verify current text carefully.
• Article 20 protects against ex-post-facto laws, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination — all non-suspendable.

solution.concept_anchor: Parliament can legislate on State List during emergency but FR compliance required
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both the Parliamentary power over State List during emergency (A) and Article 250 (R) and that R is cited as the basis for A in textbooks will mark (a) without verifying whether R is actually the cause of A or merely a co-existing power.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Yes. During National Emergency, Parliament can legislate on State List subjects — this power flows from Article 250.
Step 2: Is R correct? — Yes. Article 250 specifically grants Parliament the power to make laws with respect to any matter in the State List while a National Emergency is in force.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — Partially but not completely. While Article 250 is the source of Parliamentary legislative power over State List during emergency, the statement in A specifically adds 'but such laws cannot violate unsuspended Fundamental Rights' — R does not mention this constraint at all. R explains only the power, not the FR compliance requirement that is the critical claim in A. The causal relationship is incomplete.
Both A and R are correct, but R does NOT fully explain A — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is subtle. R correctly identifies the source of Parliamentary power over State List subjects during emergency (Article 250). However, A makes a specific additional claim — that such laws must still comply with unsuspended FRs. R says nothing about this FR compliance requirement. Students who verify both A and R as true and assume R must therefore explain A will select (a) without checking whether R explains the specific constitutional proposition in A or merely a part of it.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between emergency legislative power and Fundamental Rights compliance is a nuanced constitutional position.

• Assertion (A): Correct. Article 250 gives Parliament the power to legislate on State List subjects during National Emergency. However, this expanded legislative power does not override the Fundamental Rights that remain in force — Parliament's emergency legislation must still comply with unsuspended FRs.
• Reason (R): Correct. Article 250 is indeed the constitutional source granting Parliament the power to make laws on State List subjects during a National Emergency — this is an accurate statement of law.
• Causal relationship: R explains the source of Parliamentary power but does not explain the constraint on that power (FR compliance). A contains a specific legal proposition — that the power is bounded by FR compliance — which R does not address. R is a correct but incomplete explanation of A.

The correct answer is (b): both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• Laws made under Article 250 during emergency automatically cease to have effect six months after the emergency ends (on State List matters).
• Parliament's emergency legislation on State List subjects can abridge Article 19 only if Article 358 is operative — otherwise FR compliance is mandatory.
• Article 13 continues to apply to all emergency legislation concerning unsuspended FRs.

solution.concept_anchor: Different emergency types matched to their FR impact
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may correctly identify C-3 (partial emergency + territorial FR effect) and D-1 (Article 360 + no FR suspension) but then conflate Article 356 with some degree of FR restriction, mismatching A and B.
elimination_logic: Match A (President's Rule, Article 356) with 4: President's Rule is a state-governance failure provision — no Fundamental Right is suspended; citizens retain all FRs including Article 19 and Article 21.

Match B (National Emergency on grounds of armed rebellion) with 2: Armed rebellion is a ground under Article 352 but does NOT trigger Article 358 (Article 19 suspension) — the 44th Amendment restricted Article 358 to war/external aggression.

Match C (Partial National Emergency, 42nd Amendment) with 3: When emergency is proclaimed for part of India, Articles 358 and 359 effects are limited to that territory — some citizens retain full rights while others may have them suspended.
Match D (Financial Emergency, Article 360) with 1: Article 360 has no FR suspension mechanism — neither Article 358 nor 359 applies; confirms option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap pairs President's Rule with some FR restriction (students associate 'emergency' with rights curtailment) and pairs Financial Emergency with some financial FR restriction. Both are wrong — Article 356 and Article 360 have zero FR suspension mechanisms. The armed rebellion trap (B-2) is the most precise test: students who know Article 352 allows armed rebellion as an emergency ground may assume Article 358 still applies. It does not — the 44th Amendment excluded armed rebellion from Article 358's scope.
solution.final_explanation:
Correctly mapping each constitutional provision to its precise effect on Fundamental Rights is essential.

• A–4 (Correct): President's Rule (Article 356) governs state governance failure. Citizens in the affected state retain all Fundamental Rights — no suspension occurs. Parliament legislates for the state but must respect all intact FRs.
• B–2 (Correct): National Emergency on grounds of armed rebellion triggers Article 352 but NOT Article 358. The 44th Amendment specifically restricted Article 358's application to war and external aggression — armed rebellion does not cause automatic Article 19 suspension.
• C–3 (Correct): The 42nd Amendment enabled partial emergency proclamations. When emergency covers only part of India, the FR suspension effects (Articles 358 and 359) are territorially bounded — citizens in non-covered areas retain their full rights.
• D–1 (Correct): Financial Emergency (Article 360) empowers the President to issue financial directions to states and reduce salaries of officials and judges, but has no FR suspension mechanism whatsoever. It has never been proclaimed in India.

Value Addition:
• The three types of emergency under the Indian Constitution: National (Art. 352), President's Rule (Art. 356), Financial (Art. 360).
• Only National Emergency can trigger FR suspension mechanisms (Articles 358 and 359).
• Financial Emergency has zero proclamation history in India — a significant constitutional curiosity.

solution.concept_anchor: Emergency events — 1962 proclamation through 44th Amendment sequence
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the 1975 Emergency and 44th Amendment are correctly placed late may reverse the 1971 war emergency and 42nd Amendment, not realising the 42nd Amendment came after the 1975 Emergency, not the 1971 one.
elimination_logic: Place the 1962 Emergency: National Emergency proclaimed during the Indo-China War — this is the first National Emergency in India's history, firmly placed first.
Place the 1971 Emergency: National Emergency proclaimed during the Indo-Pakistan War — second emergency, clearly after 1962.
Place the 1975 Emergency: Proclaimed on grounds of 'internal disturbance' — third emergency; 42nd Amendment was enacted in 1976 during this emergency's continuation.

Place the 44th Amendment: Enacted in 1978 after the Janata government came to power — last in the sequence. Correct order: 1962 Emergency → 1971 Emergency → 1975 Emergency → 44th Amendment 1978, which is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is temporal proximity — students may confuse whether the 42nd Amendment (1976) or 44th Amendment (1978) is the one being referenced, and may misplace the 1971 Emergency (war with Pakistan) relative to the 1975 Emergency. Additionally, some students may know that India 'won' the 1971 war and assume the emergency was short, potentially reversing its position relative to the 1975 Emergency. The correct chronological sequence requires knowing all three emergency proclamation years precisely.
solution.final_explanation:
India has experienced National Emergency three times, and the constitutional amendments that followed the third emergency are historically significant.

• 1962 National Emergency: Proclaimed by President S. Radhakrishnan during the Sino-Indian War — India's first National Emergency. Article 358's operation (suspending Article 19) occurred for the first time.
• 1971 National Emergency: Proclaimed during the Indo-Pakistani War of 1971 — the emergency associated with the Liberation of Bangladesh. This was on grounds of external aggression and war.
• 1975 National Emergency: Proclaimed on grounds of 'internal disturbance' — the controversial emergency under PM Indira Gandhi. This led to the Presidential Order suspending Articles 21 and 22 enforcement, which the ADM Jabalpur case addressed.
• 44th Constitutional Amendment 1978: Enacted by the Janata government after the Emergency ended; replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion,' made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable, and introduced multiple procedural safeguards.

Correct sequence: 1962 Emergency → 1971 Emergency → 1975 Emergency → 44th Amendment — option (b).

Value Addition:
• The 1962 Emergency was formally revoked only in 1968 — it ran for six years.
• The 1971 Emergency was revoked in 1977, having overlapped with the 1975 proclamation.
• The 1975 Emergency is the only one associated with domestic political grounds and remains constitutionally controversial.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 359 — FR enforcement suspended but right survives; consequences after emergency
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who learn that Article 359 'suspends Fundamental Rights' will conclude Arjun has no remedy at all — missing both the six-month law survival rule and the fact that the right itself was never extinguished.
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable principle: Article 359 suspends the right to move courts for enforcement, not the FR itself. Once the emergency ends, the FR is enforceable again; laws abridging it under Article 358 get a six-month grace period, but executive actions do not.
Eliminate (a): Arjun is not permanently without remedy — once the Presidential Order lapses or the emergency ends, he can approach courts.
Eliminate (b): The FR was not permanently extinguished — Article 359 creates temporary unenforceability; the right survives and can be asserted post-emergency.

Eliminate (d): There is no constitutional provision requiring Arjun to wait for Parliament to repeal the relevant law before approaching courts — once the emergency ends, the court bar lifts automatically.

Select (c): After the Presidential Order under Article 359 ceases to operate, Arjun can approach the appropriate court to enforce his FR — the right survived throughout, only its enforcement was temporarily suspended.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario specifically tests whether students understand that the end of the Presidential Order or the end of the emergency restores the citizen's right to approach courts. Option (a) — 'no remedy at all' — is the most dangerous distractor because it reflects the pre-44th Amendment, ADM Jabalpur-era understanding. Post-44th Amendment, for rights other than Articles 20 and 21, the FR itself survives during Article 359 suspension — it just cannot be enforced in court during that period. Once the order ends, full enforceability is restored.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the precise constitutional effect of an Article 359 Presidential Order and what happens when that order ceases to operate.

Applicable principle: Article 359 does not extinguish the Fundamental Right — it only suspends the right to move courts for its enforcement during the period the Presidential Order is in force. Once the order is revoked or the emergency ends, the FR becomes fully enforceable again.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Arjun is not permanently without remedy. The Presidential Order is temporary; once it ceases, he can approach the court. Even during the order, rights under Articles 20 and 21 remain fully enforceable.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The specified FR was not permanently extinguished — Article 359 creates a temporary enforcement bar, not permanent abolition. The right continued to exist in law throughout.
• Option (c) — Correct: Once the Presidential Order under Article 359 ceases to operate, the enforcement bar lifts automatically. Arjun can approach the court to enforce the FR — the right survived, only its judicial enforcement was paused.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: There is no constitutional requirement for Arjun to await Parliamentary legislative action — the court bar ends automatically when the Presidential Order ends.

Value Addition:
• The distinction between 'suspension of enforcement' and 'suspension of the right' is the conceptual core of Article 359.
• This distinction also means that if a government voluntarily rectifies the violation during the emergency period, the citizen cannot challenge the action after emergency ends (since the action was covered by the suspension).
• Post-emergency review of executive actions that violated unsuspended FRs is constitutionally permissible.

solution.concept_anchor: India's emergency FR framework compared to international standards

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike the United States Constitution, which has no explicit emergency power provision for suspending civil liberties, the Indian Constitution has a codified framework under Articles 352–360 that specifically addresses emergency-related FR suspension.
statement_analysis.reason: The US Constitution has no explicit emergency suspension provision for civil liberties (though Article I Section 9 mentions suspension of Habeas Corpus in specific situations); India's written constitution provides an elaborate, codified emergency and FR suspension framework.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 4 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) permits state parties to derogate from their ICCPR obligations during a public emergency, but does not permit derogation from the right to life under Article 6 of the ICCPR.
statement_analysis.reason: ICCPR Article 4 explicitly lists non-derogable rights including the right to life (Article 6), freedom from torture, and freedom of thought — states cannot suspend these even during emergency, mirroring India's post-44th Amendment position on Articles 20 and 21.

statement_analysis.statement: The United Kingdom, unlike India, has a codified constitutional provision that explicitly specifies which fundamental rights can be suspended during a national emergency declared by Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: The UK has no codified constitution with explicit FR suspension provisions — it relies on parliamentary sovereignty and conventions. The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporates ECHR rights but is an ordinary Act of Parliament, not a codified constitutional provision with an emergency suspension framework.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All three' tempts students who know Statements 1 and 2 are correct and are unfamiliar with the UK constitutional position, leading them to accept Statement 3's claim about a 'codified constitutional provision' as plausible.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Correct — the US has no explicit constitutional emergency provision for FR suspension (the Suspension Clause is limited to Habeas Corpus in rebellion/invasion); India's framework is elaborate and written.
Verify Statement 2: Correct — ICCPR Article 4 permits derogation but explicitly protects Article 6 (right to life) and other rights as non-derogable.

Verify Statement 3: Incorrect — UK does not have a codified constitution; the Human Rights Act 1998 is an ordinary parliamentary statute, not a constitutional provision. The UK has no explicit emergency FR suspension framework comparable to India's.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a plausible-fabrication trap. Students who know the UK has some rights framework (the Human Rights Act / European Convention on Human Rights) may assume it includes an explicit codified emergency FR suspension provision. The UK's uncodified constitutional system is one of the most distinguishing features of British constitutionalism — it has no written constitution, no codified FR suspension framework, and relies on parliamentary sovereignty. The statement's confident, authoritative phrasing makes it appear factual.
solution.final_explanation:
Comparative constitutional analysis of emergency powers is a UPSC Mains-relevant area that occasionally appears in Prelims.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The US Constitution's only mention of emergency suspension relates to the writ of Habeas Corpus (Article I, Section 9 — suspended during rebellion or invasion). There is no comprehensive civil liberties suspension framework equivalent to India's Articles 352-360. India's written constitution provides an elaborate, structured emergency power regime.
• Statement 2 — Correct: ICCPR Article 4(1) permits states to derogate from their ICCPR obligations during a genuine public emergency. However, Article 4(2) lists non-derogable rights including Article 6 (right to life) — mirroring India's post-44th Amendment position that Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The United Kingdom famously has no codified constitution. The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporates European Convention on Human Rights rights into UK law but is an ordinary Act of Parliament — not a codified constitutional provision. The UK has no equivalent of India's Articles 358-359 in any constitutional document.

Value Addition:
• India ratified the ICCPR in 1979 — one year after the 44th Amendment independently arrived at the same non-derogability position for right to life.
• The European Convention on Human Rights (Article 15) also permits derogation in emergencies but preserves the right to life — a parallel international framework.
• India's emergency framework is considered more detailed than most democracies but also more susceptible to executive manipulation, as 1975 showed.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 358 is self-executing — it automatically comes into force upon proclamation of National Emergency without requiring any executive order.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 358 operates automatically upon proclamation of National Emergency on grounds of war or external aggression — no separate Presidential Order is required, distinguishing it fundamentally from Article 359.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 359, only the right to move the Supreme Court under Article 32 is suspended — citizens can still approach High Courts under Article 226 for enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 359 suspends the right to move 'any court' for enforcement of specified FRs — not just the Supreme Court under Article 32. However, since Article 226 is not a FR but a constitutional power of High Courts, an Article 359 order does not automatically suspend it — but the statement's claim that Article 226 is automatically available for specified suspended FRs is misleading and incorrect as a statement about what Article 359 does.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 358 suspends all six freedoms guaranteed under Article 19, while Article 359 can be used to suspend Fundamental Rights beyond Article 19, including Articles 14, 22, and 32, subject to the exclusion of Articles 20 and 21.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 358 is confined to Article 19; Article 359's Presidential Order can specify any FR under Part III except Articles 20 and 21 — including Articles 14 (equality), 22 (safeguards against arrest), and 32 (constitutional remedies).

statement_analysis.statement: While Article 358 suspends Article 19 for the entire duration of the National Emergency, an Article 359 Presidential Order can be revoked before the emergency itself ends.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 359(2) provides that the President may vary or revoke an Article 359 order — a Presidential Order can therefore be revoked independently of the emergency, allowing for partial restoration of FR enforcement before the emergency ceases.

elimination_logic: Statement 1: Correct — Article 358 is automatic upon proclamation; no additional Presidential Order needed.

Statement 2: Incorrect — Article 359 text refers to suspension of right to move 'any court,' not just the Supreme Court under Article 32; the statement's framing about Article 226 availability is a partial-truth distortion.
Statement 3: Correct — Article 358 is confined to Article 19; Article 359 can reach any FR except Articles 20 and 21.
Statement 4: Correct — Article 359 orders can be revoked independently of the emergency by subsequent Presidential Order; three statements (1, 3, 4) are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the precision trap. It is true that Article 226 High Court jurisdiction is not automatically suspended by an Article 359 order. However, the statement claims that 'only the right to move the Supreme Court under Article 32 is suspended' — this is factually wrong. Article 359 is not limited to Article 32 enforcement; it applies to the right to move 'any court' for specified FR enforcement. Parliament must separately restrict Article 226 jurisdiction by law. The distinction between what Article 359 does (suspends right to move any court for specified FRs) and what survives it (Article 226 for non-specified FRs and as a constitutional power) is extremely precise.
solution.final_explanation:
Mastering the precise textual differences between Articles 358 and 359 is essential for elimination in UPSC questions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 358 is self-executing — it does not require the President to issue any order; the constitutional provision itself operates upon proclamation of war/external aggression emergency.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 359(1) states that the right to move 'any court' for enforcement of specified FRs is suspended — not just the Supreme Court. The Article 226 High Court jurisdiction survives because it is not a FR (so Article 359 cannot directly cover it), but the statement's characterisation of Article 359 as only affecting Article 32 access is incorrect.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 358 is entirely Article 19-specific. Article 359 is far broader — a Presidential Order can specify any FR under Part III except Articles 20 and 21, meaning rights like Article 14 (equality), Article 22 (arrest safeguards), and even Article 32 (constitutional remedies) can be suspended.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Article 359(2) explicitly allows the President to revoke or vary an Article 359 order by a subsequent order — the Presidential Order has an independent lifecycle from the emergency proclamation itself.

Value Addition:
• Three statements (1, 3, 4) are correct — option (c).
• The ability to revoke Article 359 orders independently gives the executive flexibility to restore rights selectively before the emergency ends.
• Article 358 leaves no such flexibility — it operates automatically throughout the emergency and cannot be selectively applied to fewer than all six Article 19 freedoms.
